item.title: Fugitive in Venezuela Money Laundering Cases to Appear in U.S. Court
item.description:
A man accused of participating in massive money laundering and bribery schemes linked to Venezuelan officials has been arrested by U.S. authorities and will appear in court in Florida this week, federal prosecutors said on Sunday.

Álvaro Pulido Vargas, 62, of Colombia, was indicted in 2019 and 2021 on charges of laundering more than $2 billion in bribery and fraud proceeds tied to the regime of President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela. Mr. Maduro was captured in Venezuela by the U.S. military in January and taken to New York City to await trial on federal drug charges.

The U.S. attorney’s office for the Southern District of Florida announced Mr. Pulido Vargas’s arrest in a news release on Sunday, saying that he was scheduled to appear in court on Tuesday. It was not immediately clear when or where he had been arrested.

Mr. Pulido Vargas “is no longer a fugitive from justice,” Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division said in the news release.

Federal prosecutors did not immediately respond to a message seeking details. There was no lawyer listed for Mr. Pulido Vargas in dockets for the two indictments.

Mr. Pulido Vargas and Alex Saab, a former high-ranking Venezuelan official, were indicted in 2019, accused of laundering $350 million in connection with an alleged bribery scheme involving Venezuela’s government-controlled currency exchange system, prosecutors said.

Mr. Saab pleaded guilty last month to one count of money laundering, raising speculation that federal prosecutors could use his plea to strengthen their case against Mr. Maduro.

As part of the plea, Mr. Saab agreed to cooperate with investigators.

The 2021 indictment charges Mr. Pulido Vargas and four co-defendants with laundering proceeds from another alleged bribery scheme involving $1.6 billion in Venezuelan government contracts to provide food and medicine, prosecutors said.

“The allegations describe a profound betrayal of the Venezuelan people; corrupting government programs intended to provide critical food, medicine, and housing for personal enrichment,” Jason A. Reding Quiñones, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, said in the news release.

Mr. Maduro presided over an economic collapse that led to runaway inflation, dire shortages and a staggering exodus of Venezuelans from the country. The country continues to struggle with deep poverty and high food costs under its interim president, Delcy Rodríguez.

Mr. Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores have pleaded not guilty to federal drug charges in New York. A trial is scheduled for next year.

The Justice Department recently announced new charges against the couple, accusing them of torturing detainees, including American citizens. A lawyer for Mr. Maduro has said that he denies the new charges.

item.title: How California Is Using A.I. and Cameras to Stop Wildfires
item.description:
Perched at the front line of California’s fight against wildfires is a 41-year-old named Colby Nicholson and three other roaming MacGyvers in “Alert California” work shirts.

On this warm June morning, they were on a cliff 1,500 feet above the vineyards and small towns of Napa Valley. Several major fires had ripped through this area in the past decade.

Mr. Nicholson and the others peered past the toes of their boots. They pointed toward a winding, dead-end road connecting houses and steep driveways in a scrubby, miles-long chasm called Soda Canyon.

That was the blind spot that local fire officials wanted to see.

“Let’s put it here,” Mr. Nicholson said.

By day’s end, there was a 12-foot tripod holding two cameras inside protective globes, powered by solar panels and battery packs. The cameras were connected by satellite Wi-Fi and joined a growing network of nearly 1,300 remote, unblinking eyes on the most fire-prone landscapes of California.

These are the fire spotters of today — remote, high-tech cameras attached to communication towers, old lookouts or purpose-built tripods on high vantage points. Alert California’s viewpoints have become a vital tool for firefighters and a ubiquitous presence in emergency coverage. Mr. Nicholson and his crew are the ones who put cameras in place and keep them running, so that everyone else can see.

Wide-view surveillance cameras, from highway traffic cams to ski-area webcams, are not new; Alert California’s origins go back 25 years. But now, injected with the latest technology and placed in our most remote locations, these systems are increasingly the clearest eyes on today’s worsening disasters.

Since 2023, artificial intelligence has instantly scoured Alert California camera footage, spotting wildfires before a 911 call is received in most cases. Officials then use the camera feeds to monitor the fires, coordinating teams at the scene. Real-time views are available to anyone on the Alert California website, and screen grabs and time-lapse footage help fuel fire incident pages and popular apps like Watch Duty.

“This system has changed the world of response,” J.C. Greenberg, deputy chief of Napa County Fire Department, said as he watched the Soda Canyon installation. “We have instant visibility and instant information that we need to make response decisions.”

Some fires grow quickly out of control no matter how soon they are spotted. That was evident in some of the state’s biggest fires, like the Eaton and Palisades fires of 2025, fueled by exceedingly dry terrain and high winds. Alert California cameras on rooftops in Los Angeles captured the Palisades blaze, but that wasn’t enough to prevent the tragedy.

But for those whose careers and lives depend on what the cameras display on screens across the state, Mr. Nicholson’s crew delivers the view from the other end of the lens — the dirty job of providing high-tech, real-time, open-source wildfire surveillance from places humans rarely venture.

They drive tens of thousands of miles around the state each year in a Ford F-150 pickup and a van. They install and maintain camera systems on public and private land, in places like rock ledges, 300-foot mobile phone towers, water towers and rooftops.

“Most trips end up with someone bleeding,” Mr. Nicholson said. He shrugged and smiled, his usual disposition.

Mr. Nicholson has been doing this for 12 years. His role as senior engineering supervisor is to set up all the IT components of the systems in the field while maintaining a contagious can-do vibe for his crew.

These days it includes John Connolly, a talkative 30-year-old ex-Marine who does most of the tallest tower climbs; Jim Conley, a burly 63-year-old who surfs, rides motocross bikes and acts like a construction foreman; and Kai Erwin, 30, the quiet, self-described “gofer” of the group.

Their boss, Neal Driscoll, is principal investigator at Alert California and a University of California, San Diego, professor. He has a woolly mustache and looks a bit like the actor Nick Offerman in “Parks and Recreation.”

“I hire for attitude,” Dr. Driscoll said. “I want people who don’t give up, who exploit other people’s strengths and not their weaknesses and who like a cold beer at the end of the day.”

Alert California is based at U.C. San Diego and the field team works out of a nondescript building within steps of the Pacific Ocean. Mr. Nicholson pointed to the beach where he surfs.

“That’s why I love this job,” he said. “Not only do I get to travel and help people, but I have an office here.”

He and Mr. Connolly stood in a storage room lined with Costco-like shelves filled with equipment — surveillance cameras, solar panels, satellite dishes, 80-pound batteries, modems, plus wiring and cables, nuts and bolts, wrenches and clamps, sledges and shovels, and anything else that might prove useful in attaching heavy equipment to structures in the wild.

Summer is especially busy. The crew may install cameras at a dozen sites during a two-week trip, come home to repack, then do it again. Along the way, they repair cameras that have gone dark because of dead batteries, rodent-chewed cables, lightning strikes, last winter’s blizzards or the latest wildfire.

Some of the most captivating footage comes when fire engulfs the cameras. Other popular images show nesting California condors.

The network of remote sensors that eventually grew into Alert California began in 2001 to detect and communicate seismic activity around San Diego. When the 2003 Cedar fire near San Diego burned more than a quarter-million acres and killed 15 people, it was clear cameras would be useful. A local utility asked to have more than two dozen installed.

State officials, utilities and fire departments were convinced that investing in more cameras was a smart move, and linking them into one open-source, nonprofit system made the most sense. Alert California’s budget can approach $14 million per year, Dr. Driscoll said, funded mostly by Cal Fire, the state’s firefighting agency, and large utility companies.

Fire officials cite examples of little-known fires that were snuffed out quickly thanks to early detection.

“The greatest success stories are the fires you’ve never heard about,” said Falko Kuester, co-director of Alert California and an engineering professor at U.C. San Diego.

Spotting a blaze in its infancy allows officials in command centers to determine whether the smoke is truly a wildfire, and not from a rancher burning debris or fog rolling through a valley. They can decide how many firefighters to send, whether to strike by air or let the fire burn while being monitored.

Dr. Driscoll pointed to October 2017, when fires in Napa and Sonoma Counties were the most destructive in state history at the time — since overtaken by several other fires — and killed dozens of people. Two years later, new cameras in parts of the same region helped lead to quick detection and remote management of the huge Kincade fire. There was less destruction and no fatalities.

Dr. Driscoll wants to grow the network to 1,800 cameras and fill gaps in coverage. Local and regional fire officials have worrisome spots, like Soda Canyon. More and more, people request cameras on their property.

Each installation involves two cameras, in case one of them fails. They have different strengths — to see long distances, to capture crisp images at night, to see through thick smoke.

One camera is set up to spin 360 degrees every 2 minutes, capturing six frames per rotation. The other can be controlled remotely by fire officials who want to aim certain directions or zoom in tight on specific spots.

Artificial intelligence, introduced to the system in 2023, is a growing part of surveillance. Dr. Driscoll said this summer that 51 percent of California wildfires are first spotted through A.I. and the ratio is growing quickly.

“We are the science of risk reduction,” Driscoll said. “I love that phrase.”

The field team woke up at a Holiday Inn in Visalia. It had installed cameras that week on a mountaintop fire station, on a cellular tower and on an old lookout at nearly 7,000 feet.

Lightning and high winds are persistent worries on installation days. Simply reaching the site can be the scariest part. There are stories of trucks stuck on precarious dirt roads and tires hanging off cliff edges. Long hikes to the sites are not an option. The heavy equipment can’t be carried far.

On this day, the road to the work site got higher, narrower, windier and dustier before ending atop Shadequarter Mountain. The four-story tower, sheathed in peeling sheet metal, was built in 1964 and abandoned in the late 1980s because of budget cuts.

It stood 4,000 feet above Visalia and California’s vast Central Valley. There were mountains in every other direction. The view was pocked with black splotches and burned-out trees, where the 2015 Rough fire, the 2021 KNP Complex fire and the 2024 Coffee Pot fire combined to burn about a quarter-million acres.

If only the system had been in place back then, maybe the response might have been different. Faster.

In a sunny spot at Shadequarter, the crew, with the silent choreography of a blue-collar dance troupe, built the tripod — a retrofitted, off-the-shelf deer stand — and anchored the legs with 60-pound bags of Quikrete. Digging holes can violate regulations regarding historic and Indigenous locations.

They attached an array of solar panels. They bolted on a large metal cabinet to house electronics, including two 80-pound lithium batteries. A StarLink satellite receiver was fixed atop the apparatus.

A fire official mentioned that a rancher sometimes ran cattle atop Shadequarter. The crew discussed whether cows would use the setup as a scratching post.

“I don’t think they’ll tip it over, but they might break a solar panel,” Mr. Nicholson said. “Cows are heavy.”

It was decided: Local officials would build a short chain-link fence the next day.

The crew ran wires through the cow-proof conduit about 30 feet to the tower. Mr. Connolly scaled the outside to string wiring to the top. Others, climbing interior stairs splotched in rodent feces, attached each camera to its own pole in front of now-broken windows.

Back on the ground, Mr. Nicholson sat at the tripod, holding a laptop. He could see the view from the cameras. He could move them, zoom them, spin them — just as remote fire officials would be able to do. He spotted smudges on the cameras and sent someone to clean them.

With a series of commands and passwords, the cameras were connected to the system. Suddenly, anyone in the world could see the view from the top of the fire tower.

The field team snaked downhill in a cloud of dust. Mr. Nicholson and the others didn’t know where they were headed because the schedule was in flux. They didn’t have a hotel for the night and they didn’t have dinner plans.

But they could use a cold beer.

item.title: Inside Elon Musk’s $276 Million Midterm Rescue Mission for Republicans
item.description:
Elon Musk has quietly funneled more than $276 million into Republican groups and his super PAC since the start of July, building a huge turnout operation to help the party battle headwinds in the midterm elections.

The staggering amount of money makes Mr. Musk, the richest person in the world, by far the largest known donor in the midterms. Representatives for Mr. Musk supplied the previously unreported figures on his political giving to The New York Times before a federal filing deadline on Thursday.

In an effort to save Republicans’ Senate majority, he gave a total of $158 million this summer to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing the party’s candidates for the chamber, according to his team. In sum, that is one of the largest political donations in American history, and more than the group’s Democratic rival raised from all of its donors that quarter.

Mr. Musk has also built a major Republican turnout operation through a super PAC he founded in 2024, America PAC. He donated over $76 million this summer to the group, which in turn spent that much on building a sprawling canvassing program to try to turn out hard-to-reach Republican voters. The group is active in seven Senate battlegrounds and nearly three dozen House races.

Sources: Federal Election Commission filings (prior contributions), representatives for Mr. Musk (most recent contributions).

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

Mr. Musk has already given far more money, about $366 million, to federal committees during the 2025-26 election cycle than he did during the 2024 election, when he laid out roughly $290 million to help return President Trump and Republicans to power. He has given even more in undisclosed donations during both elections, according to people briefed on the giving.

The latest torrent of spending has helped give the Republican Party a financial advantage in the midterms, as well-funded outside groups like Mr. Trump’s powerful super PAC flood the airwaves with advertising in the final weeks. No Democratic billionaire is spending nearly as much as Mr. Musk, and money remains a central worry for the party in an otherwise favorable political environment.

The donations also clear up the mystery of how much staying power Mr. Musk wants to have in American politics.

“In terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future,” he said in May 2025.

Mr. Musk, who oversees a vast business empire that has benefited from enormous federal contracts, is famously unpredictable and often jumps from one project to another. He has been far quieter about his political work since his dramatic blowup with Mr. Trump last year. After months of wielding vast influence inside the White House and overseeing Mr. Trump’s government cost-cutting project, he raged against the president’s major domestic policy bill and floated threats to start a third party.

But the two men have warmed back up, appearing together at three events in the last two weeks and praising each other.

Now Mr. Musk has donated more than a quarter-billion dollars to help Mr. Trump and Republicans in the midterms. The money signals his commitment to the right and sets him up as a potential player in the 2028 presidential election, when his super PAC says it intends to remain active — the first time it has confirmed such plans.

Beyond Mr. Musk’s donations to his super PAC and the Senate Leadership Fund, his representatives said that from July through September, he had given smaller but still substantial amounts to other conservative groups:

$20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for House Republicans

$10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group supporting Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas

$10 million to the Republican Governors Association

$2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association

“If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke and borderless country,” said Andrew Romeo, a spokesman for America PAC. “These robust investments have allowed the G.O.P. apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history.”

On voters’ doors across Texas, the campaign literature carries a stark warning: “Radical Democrat socialists are winning elections all across America. Could Texas be next?”

The hanging door cards are the work of Mr. Musk’s voter-turnout operation, which deployed nearly 3,000 paid canvassers last week around the country, according to America PAC officials.

The group has devoted most of its more than $76 million in midterm spending so far to this canvassing program, shelling out smaller amounts on advertising, mail, phone calls and text messages. Much of the messaging targets Democrats, sometimes in misleading or overheated ways.

This spring, Mr. Trump’s political advisers asked Mr. Musk to reprise America PAC’s 2024 field program, a person familiar with the conversation said. Despite the challenging environment for Republicans, some party strategists believe that a field program can make the difference in particularly tight races.

America PAC relies on a few voter-canvassing firms that compete aggressively with one another for work and for staffing, according to people briefed on the operation.

Turnover in the canvassing industry is high. One canvasser who worked for America PAC told The Times that he was paid between $1.50 and $3.00 for each door he knocked on across Texas in the heat. America PAC says it has knocked on about 6.5 million doors across the country so far.

Mr. Musk and his operation, people close to them say, have been particularly focused on the Texas Senate race. The group has unloaded over a third of its disclosed spending in that expensive race, more than in any other. It is uncommon to run an extensive field campaign in large states like Texas, where television ads are more often used to reach voters.

Mr. Musk, a resident of Austin, has extensive business interests and property holdings in Texas. Mr. Paxton, the state attorney general, has investigated Mr. Musk’s opponents, like Media Matters, a liberal group.

Mr. Musk’s $10 million donation to Mr. Paxton’s super PAC came at a critical time, when the Republican candidate was being badly outspent.

And Mr. Musk’s $158 million in donations to the Senate Leadership Fund, the most the super PAC has ever received from a single donor in a quarter, may have made it possible for that group to suddenly spend big for Mr. Paxton after months of reluctance.

That is because Mr. Musk’s donations preceded the decision in late August by the super PAC, led by allies of Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, to start what has become a $149 million pro-Paxton ad campaign.

As it did in 2024, Mr. Musk’s operation is focused not on persuading swing voters, but on registering and turning out voters with conservative beliefs — especially “low-propensity” ones who are less likely to cast a ballot.

This is a lot harder for Republicans in a midterm election, without Mr. Trump at the top of the ballot.

To do it, Mr. Musk’s super PAC is leaning hard into the culture wars, especially transgender issues. (Mr. Musk’s daughter, who is transgender, has spoken about their clashes over her identity, and he has suggested that this led to his increased political engagement.)

At voters’ doors in Texas, canvassers are told to target Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor, over her record on transgender issues, according to parts of a script reviewed by The Times.

Similarly, the Musk operation is leaving literature on doors that claims that James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, has a “radical trans agenda.” And America PAC’s top ad in the state, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact, denounces Mr. Talarico over his past comments suggesting that “God is nonbinary.”

The Musk group is also targeting other Democratic Senate candidates over transgender issues, including Josh Turek, the party’s nominee in Iowa. Nationally, one of the super PAC’s most visible ads on Facebook features a man in makeup and reads: “He made his plan to vote. Did you? Don’t stay home while crazies elect radicals.” The group is running ads and sending mail on a broad range of topics, but socialism is a core theme. The Musk super PAC regularly attacks Democrats as socialist and ties them to figures like Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, according to 48 pieces of direct mail shared by Mintt, a mail-tracking firm.

Online, it is even running personalized messaging that invokes a voter’s first name. For example, in a video showing smiling Democrats: “Why are they smiling? Because Christopher hasn’t made a plan to vote yet.”

Much of this outreach points voters to an America PAC website where conservatives can learn about how to register to vote. The super PAC is pushing what it calls an “America Pass,” a digital card on Apple or Google wallets on voters’ phones that lists their registration information, along with election dates and deadlines in their home state.

While Mr. Musk is spending big again and using some tactics that are similar to those he deployed two years ago, this is not 2024 anymore.

He is in a different place politically. While he and Mr. Trump appear to be on good terms again — “our modern-day Thomas Edison,” the president called him on Thursday — Mr. Musk is taking a hands-off approach this election and does not appear as personally passionate.

He has not brought up the midterm elections or the Trump presidency much in private conversations with friends, according to people who have spoken to him in recent months. He is focused on his businesses, these people say, and he and his business lieutenants have taken a less active role in America PAC’s operations, entrusting major decisions to Chris Young, his top adviser.

And on X, a semi-reliable indicator of where the billionaire’s mind is, Mr. Musk has written just seven direct posts this year about candidates in competitive midterm races, according to a Times review, a far cry from his relentless calls throughout 2024 to elect Mr. Trump. Five of those posts focused on Mr. Talarico — and one appeared critical of Senator Susan Collins, a vulnerable Republican in Maine.

Gone, too, are Mr. Musk’s barnstorming campaign stops, like the ones he did in Pennsylvania in October 2024 or a Wisconsin judicial election in the spring of 2025. There are no more sweepstakes where he personally hands an oversize check of $1 million to those who register voters or sign a petition, a gambit that drew legal challenges.

Mr. Musk has not evidently grown infatuated with candidates this time around, as he did with Mr. Trump. The closest he came was a $10 million donation for a long-shot Republican running for the U.S. Senate in Kentucky — an investment that went poorly.

The $276 million figure is, of course, just what is publicly known. Mr. Musk has also made some seven-figure donations to support midterm candidates through groups that are not required to disclose their donors, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.

Juliana Castro Varón contributed analysis.

item.title: One Grieving Mother, Two Mariners Tickets and a Season of New Friends
item.description:
On the last Sunday afternoon of September, Rhenda Strub was bundled up against the autumn chill for one final day at the ballpark, eating Cracker Jack and sweet and spicy pickles.

Another baseball season was ending as it often does in Seattle: abruptly and too soon. There would be no postseason for the Mariners, the only franchise never to have appeared in a World Series.

A. Bartlett Giamatti, a literary scholar who served as commissioner of Major League Baseball for five months until he died suddenly in 1989, famously wrote that baseball is “designed to break your heart,” because it “leaves you to face the fall all alone.”

Yet this season, Ms. Strub, 71, found that the opposite was also true: Baseball can help heal a broken heart.

After she lost her 27-year-old son, Wyatt, to muscular dystrophy three years ago, she retreated to his room and spent countless hours alone quilting and watching baseball games on television. The constancy of baseball helped to structure her days, but the loneliness only added to her grief.

So at the beginning of this season, Ms. Strub bought two season tickets to the Mariners in Section 120, on the first base side, thinking she would regularly go with her loved ones to T-Mobile Park. But her husband doesn’t like crowds, and the rest of her family has busy lives.

So she wrote a post on Facebook — with some trepidation, she said, because the “internet can be a cruel place” — asking strangers if they wanted to attend games with her.

“This season ticket adventure is part of me finding my way back out — getting out of the house, being around people, and doing something that brings a little joy again,” she wrote. “Baseball helps me heal.”

The post went viral in April, inspiring stories in local newspapers and on the radio.

Her family worried about her meeting up with strangers. Random people also messaged her with their concerns, offering safety tips.

But her inbox was also flooded with messages from people describing their own stories of loss. A child who died. The passing of mothers, fathers and partners. Failed marriages.

And a shared love of baseball.

“I had so many people contact me with remarkably similar stories,” she said. “They have had some sort of life event that left them feeling unbalanced to deeply grieving. And they didn’t really have someone to go to the game with but loved going to the game.”

“Baseball has a calming effect on them,” she added, “and they want someone to share it with.”

Ms. Strub is a lifelong baseball fan, having grown up just outside Kansas City, first rooting for the Athletics before they moved to California, and then for the Royals when M.L.B. expansion brought the franchise to her hometown. She loved George Brett, the Royals’ star third baseman, and Lou Piniella, who played five seasons for the team.

She and her husband began raising their four children in South Dakota, but moved to Olympia, Wash., 24 years ago in search of better jobs. She had a career as an engineering consultant and retired in 2016. She then began to devote much of her time to taking care of Wyatt, whose health problems worsened steadily until he died in 2023.

By the end of this baseball season, Ms. Strub had attended games with about 30 strangers and found that the people she connected with needed her as much as she needed them. She built an online community, bringing together the people she had met in a private Facebook group, calling the project “Strangers to Friends.”

If she couldn’t attend a game — she had to miss a few when her husband, Mike, had brain surgery — she handed off her tickets to strangers who had reached out to her but didn’t know each other.

She said she was “gobsmacked” by the reaction to her post.

“I have made so many friends this summer,” she said. “I have friends that will be my friends for the rest of my life.”

Over the summer, Jack Barrie, a young documentary filmmaker from Los Angeles, reached out to her. Mr. Barrie, who grew up in Seattle and roots for the Mariners, said he felt Ms. Strub’s story of grieving in public “needs to be shared.” The two began meeting and filming a short documentary, “You Sit Here,” a reference to the words on a silhouette next to her in her original Facebook post.

Already, people are booking games with her for next season.

“I just needed something to snap me out of the fog of grief I was in,” Ms. Strub said. “I don’t ever expect to be over his death. I don’t expect to ever recover. But I have been able to find joy again.”

Others found joy through her.

One woman who has a disabled child came from Australia to meet Ms. Strub at the ballpark. Steve Hayburn, a probation officer from Ketchikan, Alaska, flew to Seattle in September after the death of his father and the dissolution of a long relationship.

“When I saw her story, I knew I had to connect with her,” Mr. Hayburn, 55, said. “She kind of reminded me of my mom.”

They met up at the stadium for the second to last game of the season, on a Saturday night. Ms. Strub walked in with her cane, her hat on sideways, a pink chain around her neck holding her cellphone. “She kind of reminded me of a gangster, the way she was walking,” he said.

They watched the Mariners play the Los Angeles Angels and shared a tub of popcorn. “It was like I was spending time with my mom all over again,” he said.

Mr. Hayburn, who grew up in Ohio and rooted for the Cincinnati Reds, added, “It helped me deal with my trauma I’ve been through this year.”

Another new friend, Sheila Cook, lost her wife, Michelle, a few years ago, also to muscular dystrophy. Ms. Cook was shattered by the loss and felt angry and confused about why doctors told her Michelle was ineligible for a heart transplant.

Then she met Ms. Strub, who explained the disease in a way that finally made sense to her. (Ms. Strub also has three grandsons who have been diagnosed with the disease, having passed it down through her daughters with a mutation on one of her X chromosomes, she said.)

“We were just weeping and crying all the way to the ballpark,” said Ms. Cook, 74, who has a dog named after Ken Griffey Jr. “It was a wonderful gift. I truly believe it was a gift from God, that Rhenda was a gift from God.”

In the middle of the summer, the Mariners honored Ms. Strub as their season ticket holder of the year. For one night, she moved up from her regular seat to watch the game with friends in a luxury suite.

She was also asked to throw out the first pitch at that game. It was a nerve-racking proposition because she had never learned to throw properly.

It turned out that one of her new friends, Liz Brown, was a retired schoolteacher who had once taught gym class. So before Ms. Strub took the field at T-Mobile Park, Ms. Brown met her near her home in Olympia and taught her how to throw a baseball.

At the ballpark on the final day of the season, Ms. Strub stood to cheer for one of her favorite players, the pitcher Logan Gilbert, who was being removed from the game in the fifth inning.

Then she continued talking about her son, Wyatt, who had enjoyed going to a ballgame with family even though baseball wasn’t really his thing. He loved online games and singing and acting, and as a teenager, he had appeared in several musicals, including “South Pacific,” “The Sound of Music,” and “Peter Pan.”

“He always played the strong voice character,” she said.

All day at the game, the Mariners played tributes on the video board for Rick Rizzs, the longtime radio voice of the team who was retiring after 41 seasons. Fans offered testimonials about how they, like Ms. Strub, turned to baseball in their grieving. Ms. Strub noted the “constant theme of healing” in the videos and “the peace they found with Rick through baseball.”

Ms. Strub thought more about Wyatt as the game continued.

He had refused to meet with the chaplain as he was dying in the hospital. Then, on his very last day, with hours left, he asked for him.

Wyatt was quiet for a time when the chaplain appeared at his bedside, according to Ms. Strub. Then he turned to the man and said, “You’re not here for me. You’re here for my mom. I need to know she’ll be OK.”

Ms. Strub nodded to her surroundings at the ballpark — the thousands of people around her, the expansive green lawn, the ballplayers.

“This is me trying to be OK for Wyatt,” she said. “I know he’s with me. I can feel him all the time. This is a peaceful place where I can connect with him and feel joy.”

Rhenda’s social media post asking if strangers wanted to attend Mariners games with her went viral at the start of the season, but rather than write about it then I had the idea to wait until September and attend the very last game of the season with her. I found she built a community of people who found solace in baseball during tough times, and that the people she met needed her as much as she needed them.

item.title: Who’s Winning the Race for Congress?
item.description:
The Republican Party’s hopes of saving its majorities in Congress increasingly appear to depend on a few possible outcomes: G.O.P. advantages in money and on the map pay off, the polls are wrong, or a major news development suddenly brightens the party’s prospects.

In the meantime, Republicans in competitive races are doing whatever they can to try to loosen their ties to President Trump’s agenda, which is dragging their party down with just over three weeks to go before the midterm elections.

There have been new ads stating opposition to Trump’s tariffs from candidates who supported them, calls to end the war in Iran from candidates who backed it and efforts to look bipartisan from candidates who pledged to be Trump’s top allies.

The debates last week made clear that Republicans are on the back foot. Questions about high prices, tariffs and the war dominated the sessions in battleground states. While G.O.P. advertising often aims to link Democrats to their party’s left-wing figures and stoke disputes about transgender athletes, cost-of-living issues are paramount to voters this year.

Trump’s rhetoric is not helping his party. Even as his own approval ratings have plummeted, he urges voters to pretend that he is on the ballot. He touts data centers that are even less popular than he is. And he has shown no inclination to back off from his positions on the war in Iran or tariffs.

But then there is the money.

Thanks to Trump’s super PACs and well-heeled political allies, Republicans still hold a commanding financial advantage. The billionaire Elon Musk has directed more than $276 million to Republicans since the start of July.

Republicans hope that will help them pull through on a House map they sought to redraw in their favor and Senate map that features plenty of races in red states. But the time to change minds and move votes is shrinking by the day.

The New York Times

Republicans have all but conceded the race in North Carolina to Democrat Roy Cooper, a popular former governor. In Georgia, Senator Jon Ossoff has a commanding lead over Representative Mike Collins. And now Democrats are on offense in deep-red Kansas, with Senate Majority PAC, the party’s main super PAC, beginning $5 million worth of ads in the state.

According to polls, Democratic candidates are leading or running neck-and-neck in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas — all places Trump won three times by substantial margins. He and Vice President JD Vance have aimed to energize the base with appearances in those states, but the polls suggest the Democrats are holding their own.

In the eyes of Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader, Democrats even have a chance to take back the majority partly because of his recruiting efforts. In an interview Friday, he claimed credit for getting Cooper, former Senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio and former Representative Mary Peltola of Alaska into their races and helping Josh Turek win his primary in Iowa.

“I couldn’t accept the map as is because the map as is consigns us to a minority, all things being equal, just because of the way the states are structured,” Schumer said. “So we had to expand the map. I didn’t accept the original map. I worked to build a better one.”

Still, some Democrats worry about Senate races that ought to be easier for them. Contests remain tight in Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire.

The New York Times

Things do not look promising for House Republican hopes of retaining their majority.

The Cook Political Report on Friday shifted 18 districts toward Democrats. Two Iowa seats, held by Representatives Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, are now considered “lean Democratic.”

That is in addition to Republicans already punting on the Omaha-based district held by the retiring Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska.

Representative Tom Emmer of Minnesota, the House majority whip, said the issue is that Republican voters may be too “satisfied” with Trump to vote in November.

“The midterms, you typically have the party that wins the White House is satisfied,” Emmer said Sunday on ABC’s “This Week.” “If our people will turn out — you may be satisfied, but that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t vote. You show up and vote, we’re going to be fine.”

Democrats need to flip just three seats to take a House majority. Many election forecasters now suggest they will do much better than that. During a discussion last week, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader, repeatedly declined to predict how many seats his party would win.

He did, however, suggest that Democrats would be able to repeat their successes from 2018, the last midterm with Trump in the White House.

“Past performance is not evidence of future results,” he said. “But it provides at least a path for us to ascertain what is possible.”

Even for Musk, a quarter-billion dollars is a lot to spend on politics in just three months.

The billionaire has once again become the largest single donor to Republican causes. The roughly $276 million he directed to groups during July, August and September means his tab for the 2026 elections is now about $366 million.

Musk’s funds are split between $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Senate G.O.P. super PAC; over $76 million to America PAC, his own outlet that focuses on voter turnout; $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, which supports House Republicans; and other donations. One of them reflects Musk’s interest in the Texas Senate race: He gave $10 million to a super PAC backing Ken Paxton, who polls show trails James Talarico, the Democratic candidate trying to become the first in his party to win a Texas Senate seat since 1988.

In five states with competitive Senate races, 615,100 ballots have already been cast.

After vanishing from the campaign trail for nine days, James Talarico, the Texas Democrat running for Senate, emerged at the Austin City Limits music festival Friday. He said he’d been home sick with the flu.

Talarico’s Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, had been making hay out of Talarico’s whereabouts. What is next in the Texas campaign is unclear: Talarico on Saturday challenged Paxton to debate, and Trump has suggested Paxton should debate, but Paxton has yet to agree to a debate.

76 percent.

That’s the percentage of Ohio voters who said Trump’s policies have increased cost of living in the state in a CNN/SSRS poll. The poll found Brown, the Democrat, up by 6 percentage points over Senator Jon Husted, the Republican. Trump and Vance have both visited the state recently in an attempt to boost support for Husted.

Trump’s latest idea to bring down gas prices — importing diesel fuel from Russia — got a chilly reception from some of his fellow Republicans, including a few in battleground races. Former Representative Mike Rogers of Michigan and Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska, who are both locked in tight Senate races, panned the idea. Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania said on Saturday that he would force a vote to block Russian oil purchases. The U.S. has forbidden importing Russian fuel since 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine.

In Maine, the cost of home heating oil is surging along with prices of seemingly everything else, forcing voters to pay more to stay warm just as fall temperatures drop.

Republicans concede the costs — up 80 percent over a year ago to fill a standard heating oil tank — are a problem for Senator Susan Collins, who backed the Iran war that drove up oil prices before she called for it to end.

“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club.” — Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia

Ossoff pulled no punches in his debate attacks on Representative Mike Collins, his Republican opponent in Georgia’s Senate race. He said Collins had “hired half the Third Reich,” a reference to Collins hiring aides who have espoused white nationalist and antisemitic views.

Collins responded that he had “condemned racism, antisemitism, hate.”
